readings.c2s3:
¶
'''upstare''' (up-stãr′), ''v. i.'' To stare or stand on end; be erect or conspicuous; bristle. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The king’s son, Ferdinand,
With hair ''up-staring'', . . .
Was the first man that leap’d.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 213.}}}}

'''upstart''' (up-stärt′), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''upsterten'', ''upstirten''; < ''up'' + ''start''<sup>1</sup>.] To start or spring up suddenly.
{{smaller block|With that word ''upstirte'' the olde wyf.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 190.}}
<poem>Her father’s fiddler he came by, . . .
''Upstarted'' her ghaist before his eye.</poem>
{{right|''The Bonny Bows o’ London'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 362).}}}}

'''upstart''' (up′stärt), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ''upstart'', ''v.'' Cf. ''upskip''.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' One who or that which starts or springs up suddenly; specifically, a person who suddenly rises from a humble position to wealth, power, or consequence; a parvenu.
{{smaller block|I think this ''upstart'' is old Talbot’s ghost.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., iv. 7. 87.}}
<poem>A mere ''upstart'',
That has no pedigree, no house, no coat,
No ensigns of a family!</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, ii. 1.}}
If it seeme strange that the Turkish Religion (a newer ''vpstart'') be declared before those former of the Pagans, etc.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 319.}}}}
'''2.''' One who assumes a lofty or arrogant tone. —'''3.''' A puddle made by the hoofs of horses in clayey ground. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] —'''4.''' The meadow-saffron, ''Colchicum autumnale'',
readings.c3s1:
whose flowers spring up suddenly without leaves.

'''II.''' ''a.'' '''1†.''' Starting up suddenly; quickly rising.
{{smaller block|With ''upstart'' haire and staring eyes dismay.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. x. 54.}}}}
'''2.''' Suddenly raised to prominence or consequence; parvenu: as, “a race of ''upstart'' creatures,” ''Milton'', P. L., ii. 834.
{{smaller block|New, ''vp-start'' Gods, of yester-dayes device.
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Decay.}}
An ''upstart'' institution so totally unassisted by secular power and interest. {{right|''Evelyn'', True Religion, II. 128.}}}}
'''3.''' Characteristic of a parvenu; new and pretentious.
{{smaller block|Think you that we can brook this ''upstart'' pride?
{{right|''Marlowe'', Edward the Second, i. 4.}}
<poem>The wronged landscape coldly stands aloof,
Refusing friendship with the ''upstart'' roof.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Fitz Adam’s Story.}}}}

'''upstaunch†''', ''v. t.'' See ''upstanch.''

'''upstay''' (up-stā′), ''v. t.'' To sustain; support. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 430.

'''upstep†''' (up-step′), ''v. i.'' To step up; move upward. ''Hynd Horn'' (Child’s Ballads, IV. 26).

'''upstir†''' (up′stėr), ''n.'' Commotion; tumult; insurrection. ''Sir J. Cheke'', The Hurt of Sedition.

'''upstream''' (up-strēm′), ''v. i.'' To stream, flow, or flame up: as, ''upstreaming'' flames.

'''up-stream''' (up′strēm′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' Toward the higher part of a stream; against the
readings.c3s2:
current: as, to row ''up-stream.''

¶
'''up-stream''' (up′strēm), ''prep. phr.'' as ''a.'' [< ''up-stream, adv.''] Of or pertaining to the upper part of a stream; moving against the current.
{{smaller block|An ''up-stream'' wind increases the surface resistance.
{{right|''Gov. Report on Miss. River'', 1861 (rep. 1876), p. 270.}}}}

'''up-street''' (up′strēt′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' At or toward the higher part or upper end of a street.

'''upsun†''' (up′sun), ''n.'' The time during which the sun is above the horizon; the time between sunrise and sunset. ''Fountainhall.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')

'''upsurge''' (up-sėrj′), ''v. i.'' To surge up. ''The Century'', XXVI. 130. [Rare.]

'''upswarm†''' (up-swârm′), ''v.'' '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To rise in swarms; swarm up.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Upswarming'' show’d
On the high battlement their glitt’ring spears.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Iliad, xii.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To cause to rise in a swarm or swarms; raise in a swarm. ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 2. 30.

'''upsway''' (up-swā′), ''v. t.'' To sway or swing up; brandish. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|That right-hand Giant ’gan his club ''upsway.''
{{right|''Scott'', Vision of Don Roderick, The Vision, st. 16.}}}}

'''up-sweep''' (up′swēp), ''n.'' A sweeping upward: as, the ''up-sweep'' of a curve; the ''up-sweep'' of an arch. [Rare.]

'''upswell''' (up-swel′), ''v. i.'' To swell up; rise up. ''Wordsworth'', Ode, 1814.

'''upsyturvy†''' (up-si-tėr′vi), ''adv.'' [A variation of ''topsyturvy'', substituting ''up'' for ''top''.] Upside down; topsyturvy. [Rare.]

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|upsend|6663|upthrow}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''upsend''' (up-send′), ''v. t.'' To send, cast, or throw up. ''Cowper'', Iliad, xviii. [Rare.]

'''upset''' (up-set′), ''v.'' [< ME. ''upsetten'', set up (= MD. ''opsetten'', set up, propose or fix, as the price of goods, D. ''ozzetten'', set up, raise, raise the price of, venture, = G. ''aufsetzen'', set up, compose); < ''up'' + ''set''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To set or place up.
{{smaller block|Now is he in the see with saile on mast ''upsette.''
{{right|''Rob. of Brunne'', p. 70.}}}}
'''2.''' To overturn; overthrow; overset, as a boat or a carriage; hence, figuratively, to throw into confusion; interfere with; spoil: as, to ''upset'' one’s plans.
{{smaller block|I have observed, however, that your passionate little men, like small boats with large sails, are easily ''upset'' or blown out of their course. ''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 244.}}
{{smaller block|She had sallied forth determined somehow to ''upset'' the situation, just as one gives a shake purposely to a bundle of spillikins on the chance of more favorable openings.
{{right|''Mrs. Humphry Ward'', Robert Elsmere, I. ix.}}}}
'''3.''' To put out of the normal state; put in disorder; of persons, to discompose completely; make nervous or irritable; overcome.
{{smaller block|Eleanor answered only by a sort of spasmodic gurgle in her throat. She was a good deal ''upset'', as people say.
{{right|''Trollope.''}}}}
{{smaller block|You needn’t mind if your house is ''upset'', for none of us is comin’ in, havin’ only intended to see you to your door.
{{right|''The Century'', XXXV. 624.}}}}
'''4.''' To shorten and thicken by hammering, as a heated piece of metal set up endwise: said also of the shortening and resetting of the tire of a wheel. {{smaller|Wire ropes are upset by doubling up the ends of the wires after they have been passed through the small end of a conical collar. After upsetting they are welded into a solid mass or soldered together.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To be overturned or upset.—{{smaller|'''Upsetting thermometer.''' See ''thermometer.''}}

'''upset''' (up-set′), ''n.'' [< ''upset'', ''v.''] The act of upsetting, overturning, or severely discomposing, or the state of being upset; an overturn: as, the carriage had an ''upset;'' the news gave me quite an ''upset.''
{{smaller block|Him his sermon ballasts from utter ''upset.''
{{right|''W. M. Baker'', New Timothy, p. 20.}}
If the Constitution is to be experimentally upset to see how the ''upset'' works, the thing upset will never be set up again. {{right|''The Spectator'', No. 3035, p. 1134.}}}}

'''upset''' (up′set), ''p. a.'' [Pp. of ''upset'', ''v.'', prob. after D. use.] Set up; fixed; determined.—{{smaller|'''Upset price,''' the price at which any subject, as lands, tenements, or goods, is exposed to sale by auction; a price set by the exposer below which the thing is not to be sold.—'''Upset rate, valuation,''' etc. Same as ''upset price.''}}

'''upsetment''' (up-set′ment), ''n.'' [< ''upset'' + ''-ment.''] Upsetting; overturn. [Rare.]

'''upsetter''' (up-set′ėr), ''n.'' One who or that which upsets; also, one who or that which sets up; specifically, a tool used in upsetting a tire.

'''upsetting''' (up-set′ing), ''a.'' Assuming; conceited; uppish. [Scotch.]

'''upshoot''' (up-shöt′), ''v. i.'' To shoot upward.
{{smaller block|Trees ''upshooting'' high. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. xii. 58.}}}}

'''upshoot''' (up′shöt), ''n.'' That which shoots up or separates from a main stem; an offshoot. ''Nature'', XLI. 228. [Rare.]

'''upshot''' (up′shot), ''n.'' Final issue; conclusion; end; consummation: as, the ''upshot'' of the matter. ''Shak.'', T. N., iv. 2. 76.

'''upside''' (up′sīd), ''n.'' The upper side; the upper part.
{{smaller block|This glass is in such a horrid light! I don’t seem to have but half a face, and I can’t tell which is the ''up-side'' of that! {{right|''Mrs. Whitney'', Leslie Goldthwaite, v.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To be upsides with''', to be even with; be quits with. ''Scott.'' [Scotch and prov. Eng.]—'''Upside down.''' [Historically, an accom. form, as if ''up'' + ''side''<sup>1</sup> + ''down''<sup>2</sup>, of ''upsedown'', ''upsodown'': see ''upsodown''. Cf. ''topsideturvy''.] With the upper part undermost, literally or figuratively; hence, in complete disorder.}}
{{smaller block|A burning torch that ’s turned ''upside down''. {{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, ii. 2. 32.}}}}

'''upside''' (up′sīd), ''adv.'' On the upper side. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|People whose ages are ''up-side'' of forty. {{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., X. 73.}}}}

'''upsiloid''' (ū′psi-loid), ''a.'' Same as ''hypsiloid''.
{{smaller block|The early condition of the paroccipital fissure as an ''upsiloid'' depressed line with lateral branches. {{right|''Buck’s Handbook of Med. Sciences'', p. 156.}}}}

'''upsilon''' (ūp′si-lon), ''n.'' The Greek letter Υ, υ, corresponding to the English ''u'' (and ''y'').

'''upsitting†''' (up′sit″ing), ''n.'' The sitting up of a woman to see her friends after her confinement; also, the feast held on such an occasion.
{{smaller block|The jest shall be a stock to maintain us and our pewfellows in laughing at christenings, cryings out, and ''upsittings'' this twelve month. {{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Westward Ho, v. 1.}}}}

'''upskip†''' (up′skip), ''n.'' An upstart.

{{smaller block|Put it not to the hearing of these velvet coats, these ''upskips''.
{{right|''Latimer'', 2d Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1549.}}}}

'''upsnatch''' (up-snach′), ''v. t.'' To seize or snatch up. ''R. Edwards'', Damon and Pythias. [Rare.]
'''upsoar''' (up-sōr′), ''v. i.'' To soar aloft; mount up. ''Pope'', Odyssey, xv. 556. [Rare.]
'''upsodown†''', ''adv.'' [< ME. ''up so down, up so doun, up soo doune, up se doun, up swa doune'', lit. ‘up as down,’ < ''up'' + ''so''<sup>1</sup> + ''down''<sup>2</sup>. Hence the later accom. form ''upside down.''] Upside down; topsyturvy.
{{smaller block|<poem>Shortly turned was al ''up-so-doun'',
Bothe habit and eek disposicioun
Of him, this woful lovere, daun Arcite.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 519.}}
To Turne ''vp so down''; Euertere. {{right|''Cath. Ang.'', p. 397.}}}}
'''upsolve†''' (up-solv′), ''v. t.'' To solve; explain.
{{smaller block|You are a scholar; ''upsolve'' me that, now.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, i. 3.}}}}
'''upspear†''' (up-spēr′), ''v.'' '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To shoot upward like a spear. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The bents
And coarser grass, ''upspearing'' o’er the rest.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Winter Morning Walk, l. 23.}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' To root up; destroy. [Dubious.]
{{smaller block|Adam by hys pryde ded Paradyse ''vpspeare.''
{{right|''Bp. Bale'', Enterlude of Johan Bapt. (1538). (''Davies.'')}}}}
'''upspring''' (up-spring′), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''upspringen''; < ''up'' + ''spring.''] To spring up; shoot up; rise.
{{smaller block|<poem>Seynt Valentyne! a foul thus herde I singe
Upon thy day, er sonne gan ''upspringe.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Complaint of Mars, l. 14.}}
On his feet ''upspringing'' in a hurry.
{{right|''Hood'', The Dead Robbery.}}
<poem>The lemon-grove</poem>}}
<poem>In closest coverture ''upsprung.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Arabian Nights.}}}}

'''upspring†''' (up′spring), ''n.'' [< ''upspring'', ''v.''] '''1.''' A vertical spring; a leap in the air.
{{smaller block|<poem>We Germans have no changes in our dances;
An almain and an ''upspring'', that is all.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman.''}}}}
'''2.''' An upstart; one suddenly exalted. ''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 4. 9.

'''upspurner†''' (up-spėr′nėr), ''n.'' A spurner; a scorner; a despiser.
{{smaller block|Pompeius, that ''upspurner'' of the erth.
{{right|''Joye'', Expos. of Daniel, iv.}}}}

'''up-stairs''' (up′stãrz′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' In or to an upper story: as, to go ''up-stairs.''

'''up-stairs''' (up′stãrz), ''prep. phr.'' as ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Pertaining or relating to an upper story or flat; being above stairs: as, an ''up-stairs'' room.

'''II.''' ''n.'' An upper story; that part of a building which is above the ground floor. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I was also present on the day when Mr. Coulomb gave the charge of the ''upstairs'' to our party and when he exposed himself audaciously.
{{right|''R. Hodgson'', Proc. Soc. Psych. Research, III. 329.}}}}

'''upstanch†''', '''upstaunch†''' (up-stânch′, up-stänch′), ''v. t.'' [ME. ''upstaunchen''; < ''up'' + ''stanch''<sup>1</sup>.] To stanch; stop the flow of. ''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 153.

'''upstand†''' (up-stand′), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''upstanden''; < ''up'' + ''stand.''] To stand up; be erect; rise.
{{smaller block|<poem>A dight vyne in provinciale manere,
That like a bosshe ''upstonte'', IIII armes make.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 72.}}
<poem>The kings of the earth ''upstand''
With power.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Ps. ii.}}}}

'''upstare''' (up-stãr′), ''v. i.'' To stare or stand on end; be erect or conspicuous; bristle. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The king’s son, Ferdinand,
With hair ''up-staring'', . . .
Was the first man that leap’d.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 213.}}}}

'''upstart''' (up-stärt′), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''upsterten'', ''upstirten''; < ''up'' + ''start''<sup>1</sup>.] To start or spring up suddenly.
{{smaller block|With that word ''upstirte'' the olde wyf.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 190.}}
<poem>Her father’s fiddler he came by, . . .
''Upstarted'' her ghaist before his eye.</poem>
{{right|''The Bonny Bows o’ London'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 362).}}}}

<poem>A mere ''upstart'',
That has no pedigree, no house, no coat,
No ensigns of a family!</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, ii. 1.}}
If it seeme strange that the Turkish Religion (a newer ''vpstart'') be declared before those former of the Pagans, etc.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 319.}}}}
'''2.''' One who assumes a lofty or arrogant tone. —'''3.''' A puddle made by the hoofs of horses in clayey ground. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] —'''4.''' The meadow-saffron, ''Colchicum autumnale'', whose flowers spring up suddenly without leaves.

'''II.''' ''a.'' '''1†.''' Starting up suddenly; quickly rising.
{{smaller block|With ''upstart'' haire and staring eyes dismay.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. x. 54.}}}}
'''2.''' Suddenly raised to prominence or consequence; parvenu: as, “a race of ''upstart'' creatures,” ''Milton'', P. L., ii. 834.
{{smaller block|New, ''vp-start'' Gods, of yester-dayes device.
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Decay.}}
An ''upstart'' institution so totally unassisted by secular power and interest. {{right|''Evelyn'', True Religion, II. 128.}}}}
'''3.''' Characteristic of a parvenu; new and pretentious.
{{smaller block|Think you that we can brook this ''upstart'' pride?
{{right|''Marlowe'', Edward the Second, i. 4.}}
<poem>The wronged landscape coldly stands aloof,
Refusing friendship with the ''upstart'' roof.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Fitz Adam’s Story.}}}}

'''upstaunch†''', ''v. t.'' See ''upstanch.''

'''upstay''' (up-stā′), ''v. t.'' To sustain; support. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 430.

'''upstep†''' (up-step′), ''v. i.'' To step up; move upward. ''Hynd Horn'' (Child’s Ballads, IV. 26).

'''upstir†''' (up′stėr), ''n.'' Commotion; tumult; insurrection. ''Sir J. Cheke'', The Hurt of Sedition.

'''upstream''' (up-strēm′), ''v. i.'' To stream, flow, or flame up: as, ''upstreaming'' flames.

'''up-stream''' (up′strēm′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' Toward the higher part of a stream; against the current: as, to row ''up-stream.''

'''up-stream''' (up′strēm), ''prep. phr.'' as ''a.'' [< ''up-stream, adv.''] Of or pertaining to the upper part of a stream; moving against the current.
{{smaller block|An ''up-stream'' wind increases the surface resistance.
{{right|''Gov. Report on Miss. River'', 1861 (rep. 1876), p. 270.}}}}

'''up-street''' (up′strēt′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' At or toward the higher part or upper end of a street.

'''upsun†''' (up′sun), ''n.'' The time during which the sun is above the horizon; the time between sunrise and sunset. ''Fountainhall.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')

'''upsurge''' (up-sėrj′), ''v. i.'' To surge up. ''The Century'', XXVI. 130. [Rare.]

'''upswarm†''' (up-swârm′), ''v.'' '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To rise in swarms; swarm up.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Upswarming'' show’d
On the high battlement their glitt’ring spears.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Iliad, xii.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To cause to rise in a swarm or swarms; raise in a swarm. ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 2. 30.

'''upsway''' (up-swā′), ''v. t.'' To sway or swing up; brandish. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|That right-hand Giant ’gan his club ''upsway.''
{{right|''Scott'', Vision of Don Roderick, The Vision, st. 16.}}}}

'''up-sweep''' (up′swēp), ''n.'' A sweeping upward: as, the ''up-sweep'' of a curve; the ''up-sweep'' of an arch. [Rare.]

'''upswell''' (up-swel′), ''v. i.'' To swell up; rise up. ''Wordsworth'', Ode, 1814.

'''upsyturvy†''' (up-si-tėr′vi), ''adv.'' [A variation of ''topsyturvy'', substituting ''up'' for ''top''.] Upside down; topsyturvy. [Rare.] {{smaller block|There found I all was ''upsy turvy'' turn’d.
{{right|''Greene'', James IV., iii. 3.}}}}

'''uptails-all†''' (up′tālz-âl), ''n.'' Confusion; riot; hence, revelers. (''Davies.'')

'''uptake''' (up-tāk′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To take up; take into the hand. ''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ii. 11.—'''2†.''' To succor; help.
{{smaller block|The right hond of my iust man ''uptook'' thee.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Isa. xli. 10.}}}}

'''uptake''' (up′tāk), ''n.'' [< ''uptake'', ''v.''] '''1.''' The act of taking up; lifting.
{{smaller block|To this ascensional movement [in cyclones] undoubtedly must be attributed the rain and cloud which we find there—rain near the centre, where the ascensional impulse is strongest; cloud round the outside, where the ''uptake'' is less strong.
{{right|''Science'', XI. 215.}}}}
'''2.''' Perceptive power; apprehension; conception: as, he is quick in the ''uptake''. ''Scott'', Old Mortality, vii. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]—'''3.''' The upcast pipe from the smoke-box of a steam-boiler, leading to the chimney.—'''Gleg at the uptake.''' {{smaller|See ''gleg''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''uptaker†''' (up-tā′kėr), ''n.'' [ME., < ''uptake'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] A helper; a supporter. ''Wyclif'', Ps. lxxxviii.

'''uptear''' (up-tãr′), ''v. t.'' To tear up. ''Milton'', P. L., vi. 663.

'''upthrow''' (up-thrō′), ''v. t.'' To throw up; elevate.

'''upthrow''' (up′thrō), ''n.'' [< ''upthrow'', ''v.''] An upheaval; an uplift: in ''mining'', the opposite of ''downthrow''. {{smaller|Where a fault has occurred which has been attended by an up-and-down movement of the rock on each side, the displacement in the upward direction is called the ''upthrow'', and that in the downward direction the ''downthrow''. As a result of this motion, under great pressure,}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
